title: Rachmaninoff, Prelude Op. 3 No. 2, four recordings
work: Prelude in C-sharp minor, Op. 3 No. 2
question: How do Rachmaninoff and Wörner move from three bass notes to triplets and back again?
intro: The Prelude opens with three low notes, A–G♯–C♯. Rachmaninoff recorded the Prelude in 1919, 1921 and 1928, for Edison and later for Victor. Martin Wörner recorded it in 2005.

recordings.label: Sergei Rachmaninoff, 1919
recordings.note: Rachmaninoff plays his own Prelude for Edison, in the first year of his gramophone career.

recordings.label: Sergei Rachmaninoff, 1921
recordings.note: Rachmaninoff recorded the Prelude again for Victor in New York, two years after the Edison performance.

recordings.label: Sergei Rachmaninoff, 1928
recordings.note: Rachmaninoff’s electrical remake was recorded in New York on 4 April; Victor released take 23.

recordings.label: Martin Wörner, 2005
recordings.note: Wörner plays in a private recording made by Tobias Lohner in May 2005.

passages.label: Opening three-note motif and chords
passages.note: The piece opens with three low notes, A–G♯–C♯. The chords that answer them are much quieter.

passages.label: Melody within the triplets
passages.note: A descending melody runs inside the right hand’s triplets, while the left hand keeps changing the bass beneath it.

passages.label: Triplet chords before the return
passages.note: The triplets become thick chords, passed between the hands and moving down the keyboard towards the return of the opening theme.

passages.label: Coda over a low C♯
passages.note: The chords grow softer over a low C♯; shorter answers and rests lead the Prelude to its final quiet chord.
